content.title: About
content.content: Beans are dried seeds of legume plants obtained after dehydration. They provide plant protein, complex carbohydrates and, when fat is added, healthy fats. Beans are widely used in cuisines worldwide: in soups, stews, salads and as flour.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beans belong to the legume family and include varieties such as kidney beans, peas, chickpeas and soy.
Dried beans can be stored for up to a year when kept properly.
Adding plant fat increases their energy value and improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Beans are rich in antioxidants, including flavonoids and polyphenols.
In many cultures beans are a symbol of abundance and fertility.

items.title: High in plant protein
items.content: Beans contain 20‑25 % protein, making them a valuable protein source for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: Complex carbs and fiber
items.content: Their high fiber content supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: When plant fat is added, beans provide monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Beans supply iron, magnesium, phosphorus and potassium.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain thiamine, riboflavin, niacin and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Anti‑nutrients
items.content: Raw beans contain phytic acid and lectins that can impair mineral absorption; soaking and cooking are required.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: Beans can cause increased gas due to oligosaccharides.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Added fat raises the calorie count, so portion size should be monitored.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beans can be boiled, stewed, baked or ground into flour. They are commonly added to soups, stews, salads and vegetarian patties. Soak beans for 8–12 hours, then cook until tender. Adding a splash of plant oil at the end of cooking enhances flavor and nutritional value.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold and nutrient loss. Discard beans that develop a sour or off smell or show discoloration.

fish-cod-baked-or-broiled-coated.title: Fish, cod, baked or broiled, coated

content.title: About
content.content: Cod is a marine fish from the Gadidae family that lives in cold northern waters. When baked or broiled with a coating, it develops a crispy crust while keeping a tender, mildly sweet flesh.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cod is one of the world’s most consumed fish due to its moderate price and culinary versatility.
The flesh is low in fat but high in protein and omega‑3 fatty acids.
Cod is a staple in traditional Northern European dishes such as British fish‑and‑chips.
Coatings can be made from breadcrumbs, flour, spices, or whole‑grain crumbs.
Cod can grow quickly, reaching up to 1.5 m in length.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of cod provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Cod contains EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other fish, cod has a low amount of saturated fat, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cod is rich in vitamin B12, niacin, and vitamin B6, all important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The fish supplies selenium, iodine, and phosphorus, which are vital for thyroid function and bone health.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including cod.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Like other marine fish, cod can accumulate mercury and other toxins; moderate consumption is advised, especially for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Salt in coating
items.content: Pre‑coated products often contain added salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Coated cod can be baked at 200 °C for 15‑20 minutes or pan‑fried until golden. Serve with lemon, fresh herbs, vegetable sides, or a light yogurt‑mint sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen coated cod at –18 °C. After thawing, cook immediately and do not store more than 2 days in the refrigerator. Store dry coating mixes in an airtight container in a cool, dry place.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-meat-.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce, Meat, and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta tossed in a smooth cream sauce with tender pieces of meat and added vegetables is a balanced dish that combines complex carbs, protein, and vitamins. Made according to home recipe (3674), it works well for lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta retains bran and germ, making it more nutritious than regular white pasta.
Cream sauce is often prepared with cream or milk, sometimes enriched with cheese for extra richness.
The meat can be beef, chicken, or turkey – the choice depends on personal preference.
Vegetables such as broccoli, carrots, and bell peppers boost fiber and vitamin content.
A homemade recipe lets you control salt and fat levels, resulting in a healthier meal.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion and stable blood sugar.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Meat supplies a complete set of essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables add vitamin C, vitamin A, potassium, and folate, supporting immunity and skin health.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: A cream sauce made with low‑fat cream or milk contains monounsaturated fats beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: The combination of complex carbs and protein provides lasting satiety and steady energy levels.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains gluten, so individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose gluten‑free alternatives.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Cream sauce can be high in saturated fat; using low‑fat cream or substituting part of it with yogurt reduces this risk.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Excessive salt in the sauce may raise blood pressure; monitor added salt carefully.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively calorie‑dense due to pasta, meat, and sauce; portion control is important for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, mixing it with the cream sauce, meat, and vegetables. Garnish with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan, or a drizzle of olive oil for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat on the stovetop or in the microwave, adding a splash of water or broth to keep the sauce from drying out.

pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce, Ready‑to‑Heat

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with tomato sauce is a ready‑to‑heat meal that combines whole‑grain pasta with a seasoned tomato sauce. The ingredients include whole wheat durum semolina, tomatoes, olive oil, herbs, and a modest amount of salt. The dish is designed for quick preparation in a microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta provides more fiber and micronutrients than refined white pasta.
The tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that remains stable after cooking.
The meal can be prepared in 2‑3 minutes in a microwave, delivering a hot, satisfying dish.
No artificial preservatives or flavor enhancers are added.
The product is packaged in a sealed film that locks in freshness and aroma.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta supplies a substantial amount of fiber, supporting healthy digestion and prolonged satiety.

items.title: Source of lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes in the sauce provide lycopene, which promotes heart health and has anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Whole grains release glucose slowly, offering steady energy levels.

items.title: Contains plant protein
items.content: The pasta contributes a moderate amount of plant‑based protein useful for tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Prepared with a small amount of olive oil, the dish is relatively low in saturated fats.

items.title: Wheat/gluten allergy
items.content: The product contains gluten and is unsuitable for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: People monitoring sodium intake should consider the salt level in the sauce.

items.title: Heat distribution
items.content: Microwave heating may be uneven; stir after the first minute to ensure uniform temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the package in a microwave (800 W) for 2‑3 minutes, stir, and let stand for 1 minute. Optionally top with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan, or additional vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep refrigerated and consume within 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanuts are a legume whose seeds are commonly called nuts. Unroasted peanuts have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. They are eaten raw, used in cooking, confectionery, spreads, and plant‑based milks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanuts belong to the legume family, not true nuts, and are more closely related to beans and peas.
They are cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, especially the USA, China, and India.
The seeds develop underground in pods after the flowers are pollinated.
Peanuts are used to make peanut butter, flour, paste, and even plant‑based milk.
Several varieties exist, including “large‑kernel”, “small‑kernel”, and “sweet” types.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Peanuts contain about 25 % protein, making them a good source of plant‑based protein.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: They are high in monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids, which support heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peanuts provide niacin, thiamine, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: They supply magnesium, phosphorus, potassium, and iron, essential for muscles, bones, and blood formation.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Peanuts contain resveratrol and phenolic compounds that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Tree‑nut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are one of the most common allergens; reactions can be severe.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Because of their fat content, peanuts are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Aflatoxins
items.content: Improper storage can lead to aflatoxin contamination; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Peanuts contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Unroasted peanuts can be eaten as a snack, added to salads, oatmeal, yogurt, baked goods, or processed into a paste. Soaking them softens the skins and improves digestibility.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store peanuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.

potato-salad-with-egg-made-with-light-cr.title: Potato salad with egg, light creamy dressing

content.title: About
content.content: Potato salad with egg in a light creamy dressing is a classic dish popular in Eastern European cuisines. Boiled potatoes are mixed with hard‑boiled eggs, green onions, and a light creamy sauce made from yogurt or low‑fat sour cream. Served chilled, it works as a side or a light main course.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The salad is especially popular during summer when potatoes and eggs are abundant.
Using a light creamy dressing reduces calories compared to traditional mayonnaise.
Some regional variations add mustard or dill for extra flavor.
It is a common dish at picnics and family gatherings.
Chilled salad retains the aroma of its ingredients better than when served warm.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Potatoes provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs supply high‑quality complete protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: A yogurt‑based light dressing contains less saturated fat than traditional mayo.

items.title: Potassium for heart health
items.content: Potatoes are high in potassium, helping to regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Keeping the potato skins adds extra fiber, beneficial for digestion.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to eggs and should avoid this salad.

items.title: Bacterial growth
items.content: Improperly cooled salad can become a breeding ground for bacteria; keep it refrigerated.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes can raise blood sugar levels, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding salt or a salty dressing can increase sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as an appetizer, a side to meat dishes, or a light standalone meal. Garnish with fresh herbs, capers, or sliced radishes for extra color and flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Stir before serving to redistribute the dressing. Discard if it develops an off smell or discoloration.
